newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian stock market seen probing higher still.
newsitem.headline: Australian stock market seen probing higher still.

text.p: Falling interest rates and an economic rebound are expected to drive Australia's All Ordinaries Index ever higher towards the 3000 mark over the next 18 months, a Reuters poll released on Thursday has found.
The poll of 11 equity analysts and economists found a median forecast that the All Ordinaries Index would firm another 1.3 percent or 35 points to 2,720 by the end of December 1997.
The index has already risen 11.9 percent from 2,400 since the beginning of January as fears of rising U.S. inflation and rates subsided and after a surprise Australian rate cut.

Analysts said they expected Australia's market would continue rising next year as a resurgence in economic growth in 1997 flowed through into profits through 1998, pushing the All Ordinaries to around 2,800 by the end of 1998.
Forecasts for the end of 1997 ranged from 2,560 to 2,765, while forecasts for 1998 ranged from 2,660 to 2,900.
The forecasts were made last week when the All Ordinaries was around 2,630 and before its mini-rally in the past week to new all time highs.
It was up 18.6 points at a record 2,692 near Thursday's close.

"I think as the economy recovers and costs remain under control you should see a profit rebound in industrial profits, and stronger global growth is likely to bring higher commodity prices and therefore higher resource sector profits," said Shane Oliver, chief economist, AMP Society.
AMP forecast the index would be at 2,650 at the end of 1997, rising to 2,800 by end of 1998.

Analysts said a large part of the forecast economy-driven surge in industrials' earnings in particular had been priced in, but Australian stocks remained cheap by international and U.S. standards in particular.
"The valuations are still reasonably attractive for our market -- not like in the U.S," said Marcus Tuck, HSBC James Capel chief economist and strategist.
"With inflation staying low and interest rates low and given the valuations remain okay there's room for the market go further yet," Tuck said.
HSBC James Capel forecast the All Ordinaries would rise to 2,750 by the end of 1997 and 2,900 by the end of 1998.
"A large part of these earnings rises have been factored in, but there's still a fair amount of it left to be put in," said Peter McManus, Equity Strategist at First Pacific Stockbroking.

Some analysts cautioned, however, that the market would struggle to repeat the sharp gains of 1997 in 1998 as the economic growth rebound fed into inflation and pushed short and long interest rates up.
"By 1998, bond yields will be heading north and that's going to put a reasonable amount of pressure on the equity markets," said McManus.
First Pacific is forecasting the index at 2,725 at the end of 1997, but did not issue a forecast for the end of 1998.
Some also cautioned that Australian stocks were becoming expensive in earnings terms when compared with the sharp rise seen before the 1987 crash.

"The prospective P/E (price to earnings ratios) on the industrial market is now 14.3 times May 1998 earnings, which equals the high reached in October 1987," John Banos, strategist, Merrill Lynch Australia.
Merrill Lynch is forecasting the index would be at 2,650 at the end of 1997 and 2,660 at the end of 1998.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
